This page describes the model before its 23 October 2026 update; an updated version follows. The "Your review" boxes save a file on your own computer; nothing is sent anywhere. Open the interactive app.

About this page: draft for expert review

What this is: a review page for a proof-of-concept model of New World screwworm zone freedom. After the last detection in a control zone, the model gives the chance that no farm in the zone is still infested, given the surveillance results. Each of its twelve parameters has a card with its definition, how its value was reached and every source behind it; each source has a card with its quotes.

How to read the numbers: every probability on this page is the model estimate of the chance the zone is free (draft): the chance, under the model's assumed rates, that no farm in the zone is still infested. Where a card says "freedom" or "six-month freedom" for short, it means this draft model estimate, not freedom as APHIS declares it. Where 0.95 appears, it is a reference line chosen for illustration, not an APHIS standard or a pass mark.

What this page records: which cards and folds you open, how often, and the answers you type in the "Your review" folds. It is kept only in this browser on this computer. Nothing is sent anywhere. When you are done, the "Your review" button at the top saves it as a file; you choose whether to return that file.

Do not cite these numbers as evidence of absence or freedom, for release, trade or reporting. They are outputs of a draft model under assumed rates.

This model cannot tell you:

  • anything from fly trapping (not in the model);
  • anything about wildlife (deer) or pets, which are never surveyed;
  • how season changes the answer: rates are summer 2026 values held constant, so a clean winter says less than the model implies;
  • anything about herds under 10 animals;
  • whether pupae and the next fly generation keep an infestation going.

The assumption behind most of the number: an infested farm nobody finds is assumed to clear on its own in about 21 days on average, a figure taken from the release rule for farms that were found and treated. That assumption and the assumed introduction rate, more than the clean surveillance, produce most of the freedom probability (what clean surveillance adds).

What we ask of you (about 1 to 2 hours)

The person who sent you this page will tell you which parameters are assigned to you. If none are named, take the top four: introduction interval, owner reporting delay, zone clearance time, within-premises recovery time. For each:

  1. Is the definition right for a US zone after its last detection?
  2. Your own value or range, in the units the card asks for: agree, widen, narrow or replace, with your confidence. Wider or shifted ranges are as welcome as narrower ones.
  3. For each source: is it good enough to inform this parameter's value? Keep, doubt or reject, and why.
  4. What is missing, including data your agency holds (for example dated case records).

Answer in the small "Your review" folds: one under each parameter card and one beside each source on it (the same fold is also on each source card). Then open Your review, give your initials and role, answer the closing questions (including whether the page says clearly what the model cannot tell you), and press Download my review. That file is the one to return to the person who sent you this page.

How it was made, and what has not been done: AI models (Anthropic Claude) searched the literature, extracted the numbers, chose each value and range, and wrote the parameter and source cards. The model's developers set the scenario and directed the work. No value has yet been checked by a screwworm subject-matter expert; the checks below are machine matching and readings by AI models. That is what this review is for.

Status: draft for expert review. Not a release recommendation.

Your note on this card

Screwworm model at a glance

Not for: evidence of freedom or absence for release, trade or reporting. Every number below is a draft model output under assumed rates.

What it is for: after screwworm has been cleared from a zone, the model estimates the probability that none of the zone's farms is still infested. It combines assumed rates of new arrivals and of clearance with what clean inspection rounds and the absence of owner reports add. Much of the number comes from the assumed rates, not from the clean results: at the central values, with no surveillance at all the model gives 0.850 at six months, and six months of clean surveillance raise that to 0.946 (what clean surveillance adds).

It levels off: at the central values the model estimate reaches 0.946 by day 60 and stays there (also 0.946 at twelve months), because new arrivals set a ceiling. It never reaches 0.95, however long clean surveillance runs; 0.95 is a reference line chosen for illustration, not an APHIS standard.

Model estimate of the chance the zone is free at six months (draft), averaged over the parameter ranges: 0.933. This is the headline as the model's design defines it: the chance averaged over 2000 draws of all twelve parameters across their ranges. The middle 90 percent of draws run from 0.824 to 0.986; 49 percent of draws are at or above the 0.95 reference line (chosen for illustration, not a criterion).

The same draft estimate at the central value of every parameter: 0.946.

Both are for the six-month scenario, whose starting state and surveillance design are fixed, not varied. The ranges are mostly judgement, so read the spread of the draws as a sensitivity range, not a credible interval. No probability on this page is a release criterion: APHIS release and freedom go by time since the last detection, with fly trapping and animal inspection.

Your note on this card

Reviewing a new model: the trust flow

1. Understand the model

Start from the picture. For screwworm: a fly arrives from outside the zone and infests an animal on a farm; on that farm, infestation passes from animal to animal (a modelling simplification: the model has no fly population); farms are found by scheduled inspection or by an owner reporting a wound; a farm clears on its own clock; one confirmed detection ends freedom and tightens controls. The picture shows where every parameter enters, so each later question ("is this number right?") has a place.

Open the model picture

2. See what the model does

Read what the model does and the agreement check: two independent implementations of the same design give the same freedom curve on 418 of 471 test settings (the other 53 could not be compared). Agreement says the arithmetic matches the design; it does not say the design or the numbers are right.

Open what the model does

3. See which parameters matter

Sample every parameter across its range at once and rank by how much six-month freedom moves. This is where review effort goes.

Open which parameters matter

4. Trust each parameter, in order of impact

Attention goes to parameters that are high impact AND resting on judgement or a guess. Nothing is removed: low-impact or well-supported parameters stay in the model and the app, they just need less review time.

For each parameter, read: its definition (tied to the picture); the data behind it and where each number came from; how well that data measures the parameter as defined (validity), how much data there is, how relevant its setting is, whether it is enough; and what the range represents (differences between scenarios, which narrow once a scenario is chosen, or uncertainty about one value).

Rule for a high-impact parameter: it needs a primary source (or two), or a secondary source confirmed by case observations, or a structured expert elicitation.

When nothing can be found: bound the value by logic (what is clearly impossible at each end), then show freedom across that whole range. A wide swing is itself the finding: freedom is not known there, the central value is not a best guess, and values outside the range are judged unlikely, not impossible.

Parameters that depend on the situation (how often infestation arrives from outside) become inputs the people applying the model set, with logical bounds and a note of why they moved them.

Open the parameter table

5. For a high-risk use, add an expert panel

When the model will inform a high-stakes decision, this AI-led review is the first assessment, not the last. A small panel of domain experts then reads it in one sitting of about 1 to 2 hours for the parameters assigned to each expert and, for each high-impact parameter, says it makes sense, it does not, or something is missing (a source they know of, a setting the review missed).

The panel can also name sources to set aside, and give their own value or range for a parameter, wider, narrower or shifted, in the "Your review" fold on each parameter card. Their answers are recorded beside each parameter and the page is rebuilt with them. Most panel reviews confirm the assessment; the value is in the occasional miss.

6. Take questions back

Each review pass turns into a short list: what works, what needs more, what the next version of the page must show. Applications tune this process; end work on a single application once the process step is settled.

The six-month scenario

Every number on this page is for this scenario unless the card says otherwise.

Zone100 farms, each with 100 animals. Holdings under 10 animals are outside the model.
FreedomAbsolute: zero infested farms, not a prevalence below a threshold.
Surveillance6 inspection rounds, one every 30 days; 20 farms visited per round; 30 animals examined on each visited farm. Owner reporting runs all the time. Streams the model does not use are listed below the table.
Start (day 0, the last detection)The number of infested farms nobody has found is drawn with mean 1 (Poisson), so the zone starts free with chance 0.37; their infestations are about 14 days old (exponential, mean 14 days). Both are guesses: no source estimates the undetected remainder.
Controls in force at day 0None is modelled. Quarantine, movement controls and sterile-fly releases are not states of the model. Spread between farms runs at its uncontrolled rate (zone doubling time 10 days, a figure for no control in the warm season). The lockdown cut, which stands for tighter movement controls and more sterile flies, switches on only at a new confirmed detection; every freedom number on this page is computed given no detection, so the cut never acts on them. In practice a zone stays under controls after its last detection; the model does not represent that, and its between-farm spread is almost off anyway (see what the model does).
IntroductionsOne new infested farm about every 130 days for the zone as a whole. The rate was counted for a free county next to an active quarantine zone during the 2026 response, and the scenario assumes that pressure, with an active zone next door, lasts all six months. It was counted per county and is applied unchanged to the 100-farm zone; no conversion from a county to 100 farms is made. For a free county far from active zones the model's settings use about 1,000 days instead.
ParametersAll twelve at their central values (the parameter table), except in the ranking, which draws them across their ranges.
Horizon180 days.

Surveillance streams: which the model uses

In the model:

  • Owner reports: run all the time: an owner notices a visible wound and the case becomes a confirmed detection after the reporting delay, which also covers the veterinarian's visit and the laboratory.
  • Inspection rounds: every 30 days, 20 of the 100 farms, 30 animals examined on each; an animal carrying larvae is found with the inspection sensitivity.

Not in the model:

  • Fly trapping: not modelled, so trap results add no evidence; it is a named later addition to the model, not built.
  • Wildlife surveillance (deer, feral swine, hunter reports): wildlife enters only as part of the introduction rate and is never surveyed.
  • Movement checks (pre-movement inspection and treatment at checkpoints and markets): not modelled; moved animals enter only as part of the introduction rate.
  • Slaughter inspection: not in the model's design.
  • Pets, holdings under 10 animals and human cases: not surveyed; outside the model's farms.

Not in the sensitivity ranking: the starting state and the surveillance design above are fixed in every draw, so which parameters matter says nothing about them.

A check on the guessed start: at the central settings, a zone that starts with no undetected infested farm reaches the same six-month freedom, 0.946, as the guessed start; the two differ only in the first month (day 30: 0.946 against 0.943). So at six months, under these settings, the guessed start does not move the answer; with other settings it might. Computed 23 October 2026 with the analytic calculation.

Fly trapping and season are not in the model: see what the model cannot tell you.

What clean surveillance adds, and what this model cannot tell you

Model estimate of the chance the zone is free (draft), six-month scenario, every parameter at its central value, analytic calculation:

SurveillanceDay 30Day 90 Day 180
As set: inspections and owner reports0.9430.9460.946
No owner reports0.7050.8480.857
No owner reports, and inspections that never find anything (assumptions only, no evidence: not a real surveillance option)0.6950.8400.850

More months do not help: with surveillance as set, the model estimate reaches 0.946 by day 60 and stays there (0.946 at twelve months as well; computed 23 October 2026). At the central values it never reaches the 0.95 reference line (chosen for illustration, not an APHIS standard), however long clean surveillance runs: new arrivals, about one every 130 days, set the ceiling, and clean results cannot rule out an arrival that came in days ago.

Why the model estimate is 0.85 with no surveillance at all: in this model an infested farm leaves the infested count on the zone clearance clock, 21 days on average, whether or not anyone finds it. New infestations arrive about once every 130 days (introduction interval). With nothing watching, the count settles where arrivals balance clearance, and the chance of no infested farm is then about exp(−21/130) = 0.85. Clean surveillance adds about 0.10 on top of that. So most of the six-month freedom number comes from the assumed introduction and clearance rates, not from the clean inspection and report results.

Why that matters: the 21-day clock is taken from the release rule for farms that were found and treated. No source on this page says that a farm nobody has found clears that fast; a reviewer's view is wanted. This and the other known biases are in one table: known biases. In this design owner reports carry most of the evidence; inspections, visiting 20 of 100 farms a month, add little (0.007 at six months).

What the model leaves out

  • Fly trapping: not in the model; trap results add no evidence here.
  • Season: the rates come from summer 2026 and are held constant; a six-month horizon runs into winter, when fly activity falls.
  • Wildlife and pets: they enter only as part of the introduction rate; they are never surveyed, and the model says nothing about freedom in wildlife.
  • Herds under 10 animals: outside the model's farms.
  • Pupae and the next fly generation: a farm stops seeding others when its animals stop carrying larvae; in the field, flies emerge about a week after the larvae drop and lay eggs about a week after that.
  • Confirmation: a detection means a laboratory-confirmed case; false alarms are not modelled.

What "free" means here

No infested farm among the zone's 100 farms. This is not the APHIS release or freedom criterion. The APHIS response strategy (the Green Book, A-1.1, page 25 of the PDF) says:

A declaration of NWS freedom after an infestation in the United States would be based on surveillance for NWS that includes trapping of flies and visual inspection of animals for myiasis. Depending on specific weather and seasonal conditions in the area(s) of infestation, surveillance should be carried out for 3 months past the last NWS detection

and gives that as generally 3 to 4 fly life cycles during an outbreak. The model's probability is at most a supporting quantity beside that, not a substitute for it.

Table computed 23 October 2026, twice independently, on the analytic calculation; no owner reports means the chance an owner notices a wound set to 0, and inspections that never find anything means inspection sensitivity set to 0.

The model picture

How to read the picture

  • Blue rectangle: a state (a share of animals, or a count of farms).
  • Green rounded box: a quantity computed from the states.
  • Orange hexagon: an event.
  • Circles in the zone: free farm (open), infested farm (orange), visited by an inspection round (dashed ring); a red star marks the first confirmed detection.
  • Small monospace text: the parameter's code name. Bold monospace: the model symbol.

Where each parameter enters

  • Mean latent time: inside one farm: eggs laid to larvae visible
  • Within-premises doubling time: inside one farm: infestation passing from animal to animal
  • Within-premises recovery time: inside one farm: an animal carrying larvae recovers
  • Mean clinical onset time: how fast a wound becomes visible
  • Share of wounds visible: the share of wounds that ever become visible
  • Inspection sensitivity: chance an inspector finds an infested animal it examines
  • Chance the owner notices a wound: the owner notices a wound (drawn as an event; it sits inside the report rate)
  • Owner reporting delay: the delay from noticing to reporting
  • Introduction interval: the zone: new arrivals from outside
  • Zone doubling time: the zone: spread from infested farms to free farms
  • Zone clearance time: the zone: an infested farm clears, at a steady rate from infestation
  • Lockdown spread multiplier: the zone: spread is cut once the first detection is confirmed
Box view (the earlier diagram)

The model has no fly population: spread inside a farm is from animal to animal. Clearance of an infested farm runs from the day it is infested, not from detection.

Your note on this card

What the model does

The what-if app used to explore scenarios runs on the developers' computer and is not part of this file. The numbers on this page come from the same calculation.

Do two independent builds agree?

Two implementations written independently from the same written design, an analytic (closed-form) calculation and a simulator (10,000 random histories per setting), were run on 471 test settings on 9 September 2026. 53 could not be compared: 5 simulator runs timed out, and 48 had nothing to compare against because no simulated history came through with clean surveillance data or the simulator's spread was zero (among them the settings with 10 or 50 leftover infested farms, where nearly every history raises an alarm).

On the 418 compared settings, 1 gap was larger than three simulator standard deviations, against about 1.1 expected by chance (2 allowed). The analytic calculation sat above the simulator in 203 settings and below it in 215, of 418 (sign test p = 0.59: no lean either way).

Agreement says the arithmetic matches the design. It does not say the design or the numbers are right.

A written check that turned out wrong

One of 18 written expectations (check 18) was wrong, not the model. It expected an old leftover farm to stay findable. In the model, once a farm is past its larvae peak the share of its animals carrying larvae falls toward zero, so neither inspection nor an owner report can find it, which is what the runs showed. The written expectation was corrected; the model was not changed to fit it.

A limit to know: the zone's own farm-to-farm spread term is almost off

Spread from nearby infested farms is in the model through the introduction rate, which was fitted to first cases in counties next to counties with cases (see the introduction interval card). The separate term for spread between farms inside the zone is multiplied by the share of animals carrying larvae on the infested farms, which stays near 1 percent at the central settings, so it adds almost nothing and the zone doubling time barely matters. The lockdown cut does not act on any freedom number at all (see below). The developers decided (15 September 2026) to keep the model and state this limit; scaling that spread by the number of infested farms is a listed option, not scheduled. The parameter ranking holds for this model structure only.

Effects in the wrong direction, all of them

Every freedom number on this page is the chance of no infested farm given that nothing was detected. That conditioning explains most of the surprises: anything that makes an infestation easier to find also makes a clean record stronger evidence. Checked 23 October 2026 on the analytic calculation, six-month scenario, other parameters at their central values; "clean" means no confirmed detection through day 180.

  • Zone doubling time (faster spread raises freedom): a doubling time of 25, 10, 1 and 0.1 days gives six-month freedom 0.946, 0.946, 0.946 and 0.947. Faster spread makes an infested zone more likely to be found, so fewer histories stay clean (chance of a clean record 0.205, 0.205, 0.202, 0.194), and the clean ones are more often truly free. The chance of being both free and clean does fall with faster spread (0.194, 0.194, 0.191, 0.184), as it should. In the ranking its average effect is −0.003, inside the range a parameter with no effect shows (see below).
  • Lockdown spread multiplier (a weaker cut raises freedom by 0.003 in the ranking): this parameter has no effect at all on any freedom number here. The cut acts only after a confirmed detection, and freedom is computed given no detection: freedom is 0.9458 with the cut at 0.07, 0.25, 0.6 or 1 (no cut). Its +0.003 is sampling noise, and its variance share, shown as 0.000, is 0.0005 recomputed with the stated method: lower than a no-effect parameter usually shows (0.0017 to 0.0083 for 90 percent of 5000 random reshufflings), a chance low, not a sign of a different method.
  • Inspection sensitivity (−0.002 in the ranking): noise. Moved alone from 0.65 to 0.95 it raises freedom from 0.9455 to 0.9460, the expected direction; the effect is small because inspections add little in this design.
  • Within-premises recovery time (a longer recovery raises freedom, +0.022): the same conditioning: 3 days gives freedom 0.908 with a clean-record chance of 0.469; 15 days gives 0.953 with 0.178. Animals carry visible larvae longer, so an infested farm is more likely to be found, and a clean record says more.

How big noise is in the ranking: with 2000 draws an average effect under about 0.006 in size, or a variance share under about 0.008, is what a parameter with no effect shows in 95 percent of random reshufflings (5000 reshufflings of the 2000 draws, 23 October 2026).

Your note on this card

The model's equations

The core of the model in plain notation, written out from its design document. Rates are per day; a time on the page (days) becomes a rate as 1 / time, or ln 2 / time for a doubling time.

Model version: a later model update changes how an infested farm leaves the zone's infested count (zone clearance) and when a farm exits it (premises exit). The equations and every number on this page are for the version before that update.

The zone: farms becoming infested and clearing

new infestations per day: b(K, t) = ((M − K) / M) × (λ + βeff(t) × K)
clearances per day: d(K) = γ × K
spread between farms: βeff(t) = l(t) × βmax × p̄shed(t)

A farm leaves K only through clearance. A farm whose animals have all recovered stays counted, carrying no larvae and so neither findable nor infectious, until clearance removes it.

Mnumber of farms in the zone
K(t)number of infested farms at day t
λ = 1 / introduction intervalrate of new arrivals from outside, for the zone as a whole (it does not grow with M)
γ = 1 / zone clearance timerate at which each infested farm leaves the infested count, found or not
βmax = ln 2 / zone doubling timespread between farms with no control
l(t)the lockdown multiplier once a detection has been confirmed, otherwise 1
p̄shed(t)average share of animals carrying larvae, over the ages of the farms infested at day t

Inside one infested farm

dπL/dτ = βw πI πS − γL πL
dπI/dτ = γL πL − γR πI
dπR/dτ = γR πI, with πS = 1 − πL − πI − πR
share carrying larvae: pshed(τ) = πI(τ)
share with a visible wound: pclin(τ) = fmax (1 − e−τ/Tc) πI(τ)

Every infested farm runs this same course; there is no fly population and no pupal stage.

τdays since the farm was infested
πS, πL, πI, πRshares of the farm's animals: not infested, eggs laid but no larvae visible, carrying larvae, recovered (treated, healed or dead)
βw = ln 2 / within-premises doubling timespread between animals on the farm
γL = 1 / latent timeeggs laid to larvae visible
γR = 1 / within-premises recovery timean animal stops carrying larvae
fmax, Tcshare of wounds visible, and the clinical onset time

Detection

a visited farm passes inspection clean with chance E[(1 − Se)J], where X ~ Binomial(N, pshed(τ)) and J ~ Hypergeometric(N, X, n)
round r is all clean with chance Lr(K): the product of those chances over the infested farms among the visited ones
owner reports from a farm of age τ, per day: h(τ) = ρr × [1 − (1 − ρa pclin(τ))N]

Detection means a confirmed case; false alarms are not modelled. The first detection sets the lockdown multiplier on for the rest of the horizon.

N, nanimals on a farm, and animals examined per visited farm
Seinspection sensitivity: chance an inspector finds an examined animal that carries larvae
X, Janimals carrying larvae on the farm, and how many of them are among the n examined (drawn without replacement)
ρachance the owner notices a visible wound (per animal)
ρrowner reporting rate per day, about 1 / mean reporting delay
Lr(K)chance inspection round r finds nothing when K farms are infested

The freedom calculation

Pfree(t) = P(K(t) = 0 | no confirmed detection through day t)

The chance of each value of K is carried forward in time. After each clean inspection round it is multiplied by Lr(K) and rescaled to sum to 1 (Bayes' rule); between rounds the same update runs continuously for "no owner report". At the start, K(0) is drawn from a Poisson distribution and each starting farm's age from an exponential distribution (see the six-month scenario). The headline averages Pfree at day 180 over 2000 draws of the twelve parameters, each draw weighted equally.

Two implementations compute these same equations: an analytic calculation and a simulator of random histories (what the model does).

Known biases: which way each pushes the model estimate

For each top parameter, the known biases and which way each pushes the six-month model estimate of the chance the zone is free (draft): "up" means that, as the model stands, the bias makes freedom look higher than it would be without it; "down", lower. Only what the cards and the model's design already say is used; where no file states the direction, the row says "open question". Sizes appear only where the page already computed them.

ParameterKnown biasPushes the model estimateWhy Basis
Introduction interval (top four)The neighbouring zone is assumed active for all six monthsdownThe rate was counted next to an active quarantine zone and is applied for the whole horizon. If the neighbours are released, arrivals are rarer (the model's settings use about 1,000 days far from active zones), and a longer interval raises freedom.stated on the scenario card
Introduction interval (top four)Which window the count coversopen questionOver the 57 days the dates span, the same arithmetic gives 76 to 127 days (shorter, so freedom lower); the literal neighbour rule gives 128 to 213 days (longer, so freedom higher). Which reading is right is not settled.stated on the card; direction from the sign
Introduction interval (top four)A county's rate applied to a 100-farm zoneopen questionThe card says a larger zone means a shorter interval. Whether the 100-farm zone is larger or smaller than a county is not stated, so the direction is not known.open question
Introduction interval (top four)First cases dated by laboratory confirmation, not arrivalopen questionStated as a mismatch on the card; its direction is not stated.open question
Owner reporting delay (top four)Two of the three timed cases leave out the owner's own waitupThey understate the delay, so their 1.5 to 2 days is a floor; the 3 days was set above it by judgement, and how far above is not known. A shorter delay raises freedom.stated on the card
Owner reporting delay (top four)A delay from areas on alert, applied after releaseupAlertness may fall after release; the naive-area alternative (a mean of about 14 days) is not used. On the card's table a 12-day mean gives 0.905 against 0.946 at 3 days.stated on the card
Owner reporting delay (top four)Veterinarian visit and laboratory not built upopen questionThe delay lumps the owner's wait, the sampling visit and the laboratory ("several days", no written source); the parts are not built up into the 3 days.open question
Zone clearance time (top four)A release clock for found, treated farms applied to farms nobody has foundupAn untreated, unfound infestation may last longer than 21 days; no source on the page says it clears that fast. This assumption produces most of the freedom number.stated on the limits card
Zone clearance time (top four)A farm stays counted after its larvae are gonedownA farm whose animals have recovered stays in the infested count until the clearance clock fires, so the count can include farms with nothing left to find.stated in the model's design (equations card)

2000 draws of all parameters together. The introduction interval and the reporting delay are ranked on days, so a longer interval or delay is the top third. Variance share near 0.005 is what an inert parameter shows by chance. Marked "(noise)": an average effect under 0.006 in size or a variance share under 0.008, what a parameter with no effect shows in 95 percent of random reshufflings; greyed rows are inside both lines. Read their signs as noise. Effects are on the six-month model estimate of the chance the zone is free (draft).

How to read the ranking

  • Range: everywhere on this page a parameter's range is its 90 percent interval: values were drawn so that 5 percent fall below the low end and 5 percent above the high end (a lognormal, Gamma or Beta curve fitted to the two ends). Values outside are judged unlikely, not impossible. Most range ends are judgement; each card says which.
  • Variance share: the share of the spread in six-month freedom across the draws that the parameter explains on its own, estimated from averages in 10 equal bins. The twelve shares add up to 0.77; the rest is parameters acting together plus estimation error (about 0.005 per parameter is chance alone).
  • A wide range ranks high by construction: the ranking measures each range as set, and most ranges are judgement. The introduction interval ranks first partly because its range, 50 to 400 days, is wide.
  • Signs: a longer introduction interval raises freedom (fewer arrivals); a longer reporting delay or a longer zone clearance time lowers it. A longer within-farm recovery raises it, because animals carry visible larvae longer, so clean results say more (checked; see effects in the wrong direction, which also covers the zone doubling time, the lockdown multiplier and inspection sensitivity).
  • Not ranked: the starting state and the surveillance design, which are fixed (see the six-month scenario).

Closing questions

To start over in this browser: (asks first). The blank offline template is on What we ask for each parameter.

Introduction interval

What this is: The average number of days between new infestations arriving in the zone from outside it (flies flying in, moved animals or wildlife), one rate for the whole zone. In the model picture it is the introduction event on the top layer, the dashed arrow coming in from outside the zone. It counts arrivals from outside the zone. As fitted, it also carries spread from infested areas next to the zone (see how the value was reached); the zone's own spread term is separate and almost off.

Value: 130 d, range 50 to 400 d (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom +0.081.

What the value rests on: counted from reports First cases counted from news reports and a public case compilation, then divided by a window and a judged number of at-risk counties; fails the page's rule for a high-impact parameter.

Quote check on this card's sources: 4 quotes: 4 found word for word. See where it enters the model picture

How the value was reached

The chosen 130 days (range 50 to 400) is for a free county next to an active zone. The AI literature review dated every Texas county's first case in summer 2026 [C-2.1, C-2.2, C-2.7a, C-2.7b]. Six far-apart counties seeded within ten days of the first case, and one later far jump (Jim Hogg, 25 June), were set aside as spread before anyone knew. Nine later first cases (20 June to 16 August) all bordered an active quarantine zone and were counted as introductions, so spread from infested areas next door is part of this rate. Nine events over the AI literature review's 85-day window, spread across 12 to 20 at-risk counties, gives 0.005 to 0.009 per county per day, a mean interval of 110 to 190 days; 130 was picked inside that. The nine dates span 57 days (20 June to 16 August), and the review does not say what the 85 days covers; over 57 days the same arithmetic gives 76 to 127 days, below the chosen 130 (recomputed 23 October 2026). Read literally, as a county sharing a border with a county that already had a case, the rule would drop Medina County: none of its neighbours had a confirmed case by its 24 June first case (Uvalde's came on 29 June), though Uvalde had been in a quarantine zone since 3 June [C-2.2]. That leaves eight events, 0.0047 to 0.0078 per county per day over the 85 days, an interval of 128 to 213 days, with the chosen 130 at the lower edge (source census, 23 October 2026). The Medina date is in the case compilation [C-2.1] and in a dated case list relaying the USDA dashboard [C-2.2]; the other news article cited with it gives no Medina date [C-2.7b]. The 12 to 20 at-risk counties is the AI literature review's judgement; no source gives the ring. Mismatch: a first case is dated by laboratory confirmation, not by arrival, and a county is not necessarily the model's zone; a larger zone means a shorter interval. The range ends are judgement. A model paper's seeding rate [C-2.6] was used only as a consistency check. High-impact rule: this is the top parameter (about half the variance in six-month freedom) and it fails the page's own rule for high-impact parameters (step 4 of the review process): its evidence is a public compilation and news reports, with no primary source and no expert elicitation. Official case records with dates would fix that. Source caution: every case date behind the count comes through a public online encyclopedia's case table [C-2.1] and a syndicated news article [C-2.2], and no quote on file carries those dates; the 4 found quotes on this card's sources are context (long-distance spread [C-2.4], a model's seeding rate [C-2.6]), not the dates that were counted.

What the sources do not tell us

Which introductions were moved animals versus flies, and whether the at-risk ring was really 12 to 20 counties: no official linkage of any 2026 case is in the files.

Owner reporting delay

What this is: How fast a wound the owner has noticed becomes a confirmed detection, set as a daily rate; one over the rate is the mean delay in days. In the model picture it is the reporting delay arrow on the bottom layer, from "Owner notices a wound" to the owner-report hazard, which feeds the owner report on the top layer. It starts when the owner notices (the time for a wound to become visible and to be noticed is not in it) and it ends at confirmation, not at the owner's call: the model treats a detection as a confirmed one and has no separate laboratory step, so the time from the call to laboratory confirmation sits inside this delay.

What the delay covers

A breakdown given by domain experts at a review on 24 September 2026 has four parts; the model lumps the last three into one delay, so the name "owner reporting delay" undersells it:

  1. Fly to noticing: from egg laying until the owner sees a wound. Not in this delay: the latent time and the chance a sick animal is noticed cover it.
  2. Owner waits: the owner has seen something but looks closely days later. In this delay.
  3. Vet sampling: a veterinarian or official comes out to sample and ships it. In this delay.
  4. Lab: from receipt to confirmation, "several days" (stated at the same review; no written source yet). One 2026 preprint reports 3 to 7 day testing bottlenecks (Garcia, abstract only, a background claim, not a measurement). In this delay.

The parts are not yet built up into the 3 days; a reviewer's estimate of each part is wanted.

How much it matters

Quote check on this card's sources: 7 quotes: 6 found word for word, 1 near match. See where it enters the model picture

How the value was reached

The chosen value is a mean delay of 3 days (rate 0.33 per day), range 1 to 12.5 days (rates 1.0 to 0.08 per day). Three timed cases were found. The Zavala County calf: the ranch manager found the wound on a routine check and the laboratory confirmed it 2.5 days later [B-3.7]; this is the only one timed from the owner. A household dog from Lea County, New Mexico, seen at a veterinary clinic in Andrews County, Texas on Saturday 6 June 2026 [B-3.19]: the news report gives confirmation on Monday 8 June, but a case table based on APHIS data dates it 7 June [C-2.1], so the interval is 1 to 2 days. Its clock starts at the clinic, so the owner's own delay is missing, and with the dog's travel history unknown the case is perhaps better read as evidence of an introduction. Sabinas Hidalgo, Mexico: a heifer recently moved to a certified feedlot was detected officially on 20 September 2025 and confirmed on 21 September, 1 day [B-3.10, B-3.9]; it was not an owner report, so it times only the sampling and laboratory part. Texas rules ask for a report within 24 hours of a suspect case [B-3.8]: what owners are required to do, not a measured delay. Mismatch: two of the three intervals leave out the owner's step, so they understate the delay; their average, about 1.5 to 2 days, is a floor, not an estimate. All three come from areas on alert during an active response, while the six-month scenario applies the same 3 days after release, when alertness may have fallen; the AI literature review's alternative for a naive area, from Florida 2016, is a rate of 0.07 per day (a mean of about 14 days) and is not used in the headline. The 3 days and the 12.5-day upper end are the AI literature review's judgement. It matters: a 2-day mean gives six-month freedom 0.956, a 3-day mean 0.946.

What the sources do not tell us

How long owners actually wait between first noticing a wound and calling it in: no per-case dates of noticing, reporting and confirmation are in the files.

Zone clearance time

What this is: The average number of days an infested farm stays in the zone's infested count before it is removed. In the model picture it is the clearance event on the top layer (an orange farm turning free again). It runs at a steady rate from the day the farm is infested, whatever its age and whether or not it has been found; animals recovering inside the farm (bottom layer) do not remove it. The 21 day value comes from the release rule for found and treated farms.

Value: 21 d, range 7 to 40 d (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom -0.034.

What the value rests on: judgement within data An agency release rule plus news snapshots of active cases; they time paperwork, not biology; the tails are judgement.

Quote check on this card's sources: 8 quotes: 7 found word for word, 1 near match. See where it enters the model picture

How the value was reached

The chosen value is 21 days, range 7 to 40. It comes from two things. First, the release rule: a treated animal is re-inspected 24 hours after treatment and released once no live larvae remain and an official veterinarian signs off [C-3.1], and the Green Book keeps animals in quarantine until the wounds heal [C-3.2]. Second, how long Texas 2026 cases stayed on the active list, read from news snapshots of active counts on 30 June, 6 August, 18 August and 3 September [C-2.2, B-2.22, B-2.17, A-3.18]: each case is only bracketed between two dates (for example 25 to 62 days, or 0 to 19 days), not timed. A fit that treats each of 46 Texas cases as such a bracket (interval-censored maximum likelihood, source census, 23 October 2026) gives a mean of 18.7 days with an exponential curve and 20.1 days with a lognormal (median 14.8 days); the spread is wide. The 3 September count of four active cases is the AI literature review's reading, because that tracker page has since been overwritten. Mismatch: this is the administrative clock, not the biology. The first Texas calf's wound healed in a week [B-3.7], and its case was off the active list by 30 June [C-2.2], at most 27 days after its 3 June confirmation; no source says how much sooner. The times are also per animal case, interval-censored, not per premises. A 21-day Texas release rule seen only in a search summary could not be verified. The tails (7 and 40 days) are judgement, set low-confidence by the AI literature review.

What the sources do not tell us

When a cleared premises actually stops producing flies, which is what matters for spread: the release rule and case lists time paperwork, not fly output.

The parameter

Your value, in days:

This card

DRAFT Draft model output under assumed rates; not evidence of freedom or absence.

Within-premises recovery time

What this is: The average number of days one animal carries live larvae, until treatment, the larvae leaving, or death ends it. In the model picture it is the "infestation ends" arrow on the bottom layer, from Carrying larvae to Recovered. It moves animals only: the farm stays in the zone's infested count until zone clearance removes it.

Value: 7 d, range 3 to 15 d (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom +0.022.

What the value rests on: judgement within data Sources bound the treated and untreated courses; the 7-day mix of the two is a modelling choice.

Quote check on this card's sources: 12 quotes: 10 found word for word, 2 near matches. See where it enters the model picture

How the value was reached

The chosen value is 7 days, range 3 to 15. Larvae feed 5 to 7 days after hatching and then leave the wound [A-3.1, A-3.2, A-3.4]. Untreated wounds attract more egg-laying and the animal dies in 5 to 10 days [A-3.4], 7 to 10 [A-3.7], 7 to 14 [A-3.8], or one to two weeks [A-3.1]; the AI literature review put the untreated larvae-bearing period at 6 to 12 days, central 10. In a trial, doramectin given 2 hours before first-stage larvae were placed in wounds cleared them within 24 to 48 hours [A-3.13]; that is preventive dosing against young larvae, not treatment of an established wound, so it bounds the treated course only loosely (the federal procedure's re-inspection 24 hours after treatment [C-3.1] is closer). On that reading an animal found on day 3 to 5 and treated carries larvae 3 to 6 days. The 7 days is a mix of treated and untreated animals under surveillance; the mix is a modelling choice, not data. Figures that time something else were set aside as too long: the 15 to 17 days of a Mexico model's "infection process" [A-3.12] (the paper gives no end point; reading it as running to wound healing is the AI literature review's) and the roughly 22 days of Mexico's active-case list [A-3.17] both run to wound healing. Open: if the model already removes reported animals by treatment, the AI literature review recommends 10 days (6 to 17) for the undetected course instead.

What the sources do not tell us

The real share of infested animals that get treated early versus left alone, which sets the 7-day mix: not in the files.

Chance the owner notices a wound

What this is: The chance that an owner notices a visible screwworm wound on an infested animal. In the model picture it is the noticing arrow on the bottom layer, from "Share with a visible wound" to "Owner notices a wound". It applies only to wounds that have already become visible (the visible-wound ramp comes before it); the time from noticing to confirmation is the separate reporting delay. In the model it is a per-animal chance inside the owner-report rate: at each moment the farm reports at the reporting rate times the chance that at least one of its visible wounds is noticed (see the equations card). It is not a one-time draw of whether a wound is ever noticed.

Value: 0.70, range 0.45 to 0.90 (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom +0.010.

What the value rests on: guessed No study measures it; bounded by indirect numbers.

Quote check on this card's sources: 7 quotes: 6 found word for word, 1 not found (not shown). See where it enters the model picture

How the value was reached

The chosen value is 0.70, range 0.45 to 0.90. No study measures it; it is a judgement bounded by indirect numbers. Mexico handled 10,511 animal myiasis reports from 1 January 2024 to 1 November 2025, and larvae from 9,049 of them were identified as screwworm [B-2.7]; set against the 9,574 cases the same bulletin confirms to the same end date (counted from 21 November 2024, when the outbreak's case count starts), the ratio is about 95 percent. That is identifications from reports per confirmed case, not the share of cases found through reports: one case can give several reports, and the two counts start on different dates: that shows most cases are found through owners and veterinarians, but it cannot say how many infested animals nobody reported, because those appear in neither count. In Florida 2016, 3 of 9 pet cases (33 percent) surfaced only through a later questionnaire [B-2.1]: these were animals veterinarians had seen, so this measures missed reporting in a naive area, not owners failing to notice. For wild Key deer, biologists estimated one undetected death per known one [B-2.2]: carcass finding in wildlife, not a handled herd. Handling frequency comes from a 2015 online forum thread of small cattle producers, with answers from daily to weekly [B-2.18] (the AI literature review's tally of 17 US posters does not reproduce: the saved page has about 15 answers that give a frequency, two of them from Canada), and a daily-check recommendation [B-2.19]. Mismatch: none of these numbers is the per-animal chance the model needs. The central value and both range ends are judgement; the verdict on file is guessed.

What the sources do not tell us

What fraction of infested animals in an alert commercial herd go unnoticed: no study in the files measures it.

Within-premises doubling time

What this is: How fast infestation spreads between animals on one farm, set as a doubling time before any animals recover. In the model picture it is the "spread on the farm" arrow on the bottom layer, from Not infested to Eggs laid, driven by the dashed loop from animals carrying larvae. It stands in for the local flies; the model has no fly population and no pupal stage.

What it implies (derived, not an input): this value is a gross rate, before animals recover. With latent time 2 days and recovery 7 days at their central values, the net doubling time of a farm's infestation is about 81 days, and each infested animal leads to 1.08 more (the outbreak on a farm grows only above 1). Across this card's range (3 to 8 days) that number runs from 0.61 to 1.62, so the slow end of the range describes an infestation that dies out on its own. Reviewers judging this value may find the net figure easier to compare with field reports than the gross one.

Value: 4.5 d, range 3 to 8 d (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom -0.010.

What the value rests on: converted from a related setting Growth rates of wild deer deaths and of fly populations, converted by a formula to spread between animals on one farm; no direct measurement.

Quote check on this card's sources: 10 quotes: 10 found word for word. See where it enters the model picture

How the value was reached

The chosen value is 4.5 days, range 3 to 8. It is derived, not observed. Observed doublings of case counts are net of recovery: the uncontrolled Key deer deaths (4, 7, 20, 96 per month, July to October 2016) double every 13 to 20 days [A-5.8]; a five-fold rise per fly generation, Knipling's design assumption [A-5.2], over a generation of about 21 days [A-5.4] doubles every 9 days; a fly-population model gives a potential 14 days [A-5.1]. The model's parameter is the gross rate, so the recovery rate was added back: gross doubling = 1 / (1/net doubling + 1/(0.69 x recovery time)), with recovery 7 to 14 days. With net doubling 9 to 20 days and recovery 7 to 14 days the formula gives 3.2 to 6.5 days (recomputed 23 October 2026); the review's table also has a row with net 30 days and recovery 15 days, outside those inputs, which gives 7.7 days. The range 3 to 8 takes in that row; central 4.5. Mismatch: the deer series (the same report and series is the main input to the zone doubling time [C-1.4], for spread between farms) counts deaths of wild deer across whole islands, and the other two are fly-population growth, not animals on one premises. The formula is the AI literature review's, and the model's instant recruitment ignores the 18 to 24 day fly generation, so early growth runs fast. Texas 2026 (47 cases on 38 premises) [A-5.13a] was a consistency check only.

What the sources do not tell us

Any direct measurement of spread between animals on one premises: none is in the files.

Share of wounds visible

What this is: The share of infested animals whose wound eventually becomes visible to someone looking carefully; the rest sit in hidden places such as nostrils, genitals or deep pockets. In the model picture it is the ceiling of the visible-wound ramp on the bottom layer, from "Share carrying larvae" to "Share with a visible wound". It acts on owner reporting only; inspection uses its own chance, the inspection sensitivity.

Value: 0.9, range 0.75 to 0.98 (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom +0.007.

What the value rests on: judgement within data No study counts hidden infestations; an estimate from site tallies of found cases.

Quote check on this card's sources: 6 quotes: 5 found word for word, 1 not found (not shown). See where it enters the model picture

How the value was reached

The chosen value is 0.9, range 0.75 to 0.98. No study counts how many infestations stay hidden on a careful look. Reference texts all name the same hard sites: nostrils, anus, prepuce, vagina and deep pocket wounds, where slight movement may be the only sign [A-4.1, A-4.2, A-4.3]. A Colombian cattle study lists barbed-wire injuries in 32.7 percent of 49 cases and navel and scrotum in 18.4 percent each [A-4.4]; the AI literature review read this as 70 percent or more of cases at plainly visible sites. Newborns are an estimated 80 percent of potential livestock cases, mostly at the navel [A-4.7]. Mismatch: a site tally only includes cases someone found, so hidden cases are missing from it and the visible share is pushed up; the Colombian quote was also not found verbatim, and wire injury is a cause while navel and scrotum are sites, so the sum may double count. The 0.9 and its range are an educated estimate; the AI literature review calls it that. Note: the hidden share here (10 percent at the central value) and the 15 to 25 percent at hidden sites assumed on the inspection sensitivity card are two separate judgements and do not agree; a reviewer's view on which is closer is wanted.

What the sources do not tell us

How many infestations stay hidden on a careful look at a US herd: no study in the files counts them.

Mean latent time

What this is: The average number of days from eggs laid in a wound to larvae present and visible. In the model picture it is the "egg to visible larvae" arrow on the bottom layer, from Eggs laid to Carrying larvae. An animal still in the eggs-laid state cannot be found by inspection and does not pass infestation on.

Value: 2 d, range 1 to 3 d (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom -0.007.

What the value rests on: judgement within data Life-history summaries agree on 1 to 3 days; the two trials time wounding to detection, so they bound it only loosely.

Quote check on this card's sources: 7 quotes: 6 found word for word, 1 not found (not shown). See where it enters the model picture

How the value was reached

The chosen value is 2 days, range 1 to 3. Eggs hatch in 10 to 12 hours [A-1.1], 12 to 24 hours [A-1.2, A-1.3] or 10 to 21 hours [A-1.4]. Larvae are hard to see for the first day or two [A-1.3] and visible by the third day [A-1.1]; disease can show as early as 1 to 2 days after egg laying [A-1.2]. Two field trials with regular inspection found infestations by day 3 to 5 after wounding in Mexico [A-1.7] (those early detections were in the ivermectin group, where the drug failed; untreated controls were infested by day 8, as on the clinical onset card) and in 9 of 10 untreated castration wounds by the day-3 check in Argentina [A-1.8]. Mismatch, minor: the trials count from the day of wounding, not the day eggs were laid, so day 3 to 5 is an upper bound on latency plus the time to notice; the Mexican authors also found larvae older than expected, which suggests young larvae were being missed. The life-history sources agree on 1 to 3 days, and the trials are consistent with it without timing it, so 2 days (1 to 3) is supported; the range ends match the life-history sources' span. The Argentine quote on file was not found verbatim in the source.

What the sources do not tell us

How latency shifts with Texas temperatures: temperature is noted to move hatching by hours, but no Texas measurement is in the files.

Mean clinical onset time

What this is: How many days it takes for an infested wound to become obvious to an observer; the visible share of wounds ramps up on this time scale. In the model picture it sets the speed of the visible-wound ramp on the bottom layer, beside its ceiling, the share of wounds visible. Its clock runs from the day the farm was infested, not from the day each animal first carried larvae, and it feeds owner reporting only.

Value: 3 d, range 1.5 to 6 d (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom -0.003.

What the value rests on: judgement within data No study measures it; trials only bound it. Known mismatch: the model's clock starts earlier than the review intended.

Quote check on this card's sources: 5 quotes: 4 found word for word, 1 not found (not shown). See where it enters the model picture

How the value was reached

The chosen value is 3 days, range 1.5 to 6. No study measures how long owners take to notice. Under daily chute inspection, infestations were found on day 3 to 5 after wounding [A-2.4], and 9 of 10 untreated castration wounds were obviously infested at the day-3 check [A-2.5]. Both trials looked on fixed days (the Argentine one on days 3, 6 and 13 only), and the Mexican day 3 to 5 detections were in the ivermectin group, where the drug failed; the abstract gives untreated controls infested on day 8. So the trials show wounds obvious by day 3 to 5 after wounding and say nothing about shorter times. On extensive range, herds are mustered only every few days [A-2.7], and observers rely on odour [A-2.2] and animals leaving the herd [A-2.3]. A 3-day mean after larvae appear, with 1.5 to 6 days, was chosen to span both; the ends are judgement. Mismatch: the AI literature review meant 3 days from the start of the larvae-bearing stage, but the model's ramp runs on the premises' age since infestation, which already includes the roughly 2-day latent period. So in the model wounds become obvious sooner after larvae appear than the review intended, by about the 2-day latent time, which makes owner detection look faster and freedom higher.

What the sources do not tell us

How many days a Texas rancher on extensive range actually takes to spot a wound: no study in the files measures it.

Lockdown spread multiplier

What this is: The factor by which spread between farms is cut once the first detection is confirmed, standing for sterile-fly releases plus movement controls; 1 means no cut. In the model picture it is the "after first detection" line under the spread event on the top layer, switched on at the red star. In the model's formula it cuts spread between farms only; introductions from outside and spread inside a farm are not changed. Every freedom number on this page is computed given no confirmed detection, so this cut never acts on them: freedom is the same whatever its value (checked 23 October 2026 on the analytic calculation).

Value: 0.25, range 0.07 to 0.6 (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom +0.003.

What the value rests on: operating setting A control setting informed by sterile-fly literature; almost no effect in this model.

Quote check on this card's sources: 9 quotes: 7 found word for word, 2 with no full text to check. See where it enters the model picture

How the value was reached

The chosen value is 0.25, range 0.07 to 0.6. It is set as an operating setting, not a literature value; a formal extraction is planned for a later phase. Released sterile flies at 9 to 1 leave only 10 percent of females laying fertile eggs, and at least 10 to 1 is the working rule [C-4.1]. The effect lags a fly generation: in Florida the last fertile fly was caught 27 days after releases began [C-4.4]. Averaging over a 90-day lockdown of about four life cycles, the AI literature review computed about 0.3 for the fly part, using per-generation factors (1, 0.15, 0.03, 0.01) whose origin is not in the files. Movement permits cut the animal-movement part to perhaps 0.1 to 0.3, a judgement. The Green Book says long-distance movement of the fly is generally a result of moving an infested animal [C-2.4], an entry for the same document as C-4.7a; that covers long-distance spread only, not local spread by flies, which permits do not touch. Texas 2026 active-case counts [C-2.2, B-2.22, B-2.17, A-3.18] gave 0.06 to 0.5. Mismatch: Texas already had sterile flies from February, so its 'before' was not uncontrolled. In this model structure spread between premises is almost nil, so this setting has almost no effect.

What the sources do not tell us

The effect of a response that starts from no sterile flies at all, the clean before-and-after the setting assumes: no such series is in the files.

Zone doubling time

What this is: How fast the number of infested farms in the zone would grow with no control, set as a doubling time before cleared farms are subtracted. In the model picture it is the spread event on the top layer, multiplied by the share of animals carrying larvae on the infested farms. That share is small in the current settings, so this spread is weak and the parameter barely moves freedom.

Value: 10 d, range 6 to 25 d (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom -0.003.

What the value rests on: converted from a related setting The growth of one wild deer death series, converted by a formula to spread between farms; almost no effect in this model.

Quote check on this card's sources: 6 quotes: 3 found word for word, 2 near matches, 1 not found (not shown). See where it enters the model picture

How the value was reached

The chosen value is 10 days, range 6 to 25. It is derived from one series. Key deer deaths rose from 4 in July to 20 in September 2016 with no control, a net growth of 0.026 per day, doubling every 26 days; July to October gives 20 days [C-1.4]. The AI literature review took a net 24 days. The model's rate is gross, so the clearance rate (1/21 to 1/30 per day) was added back, giving 0.06 to 0.08 per day, a gross doubling of 9 to 12 days, central 10. The 54 to 139 days in a fly-population model [C-1.1] was set aside: it comes from mark-recapture work on an established Costa Rican population in balance [C-1.2], not an invasion. Mexico's national counts, doubling every 63 then 144 days, bound it from above [C-1.5]. Mismatch: the series counts wild deer deaths on islands, not infested premises. The same Key deer series, from the same report, is also the main input to the within-premises doubling time [A-5.8], for a different process. The range ends are judgement. In this model structure spread between premises is almost nil, so this value has no effect on the answer.

What the sources do not tell us

How fast infested premises multiply in an uncontrolled US livestock setting: the only series in the files is wild deer.

It applies only to animals carrying larvae (eggs not yet hatched are missed) and plays no part in owner reporting.

Value: 0.85, range 0.65 to 0.95 (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom -0.002.

What the value rests on: guessed No study measures it for this fly; a weighted guess.

Quote check on this card's sources: 6 quotes: 6 found word for word. See where it enters the model picture

How the value was reached

The chosen value is 0.85, range 0.65 to 0.95. No study measures it for this fly; it is a weighted guess. Inspection protocols require a whole-body look including mucous membranes and genitals [B-1.2], larvae are visible from day 3, and deep wounds may show only movement [B-1.1]. The AI literature review assumed 15 to 25 percent of infestations sit at hidden sites, based on Mexican cases found in an ear and a prepuce [B-1.7] and the protocol lists, with sensitivity about 0.6 there and 0.95 at visible sites, giving 0.85 to 0.9. The 15 to 25 percent, the 0.6 and the 0.95 are judgement, not measurements. The 15 to 25 percent hidden share does not agree with the 10 percent on the share of wounds visible card; the two are separate judgements. The nearest data are for the Old World screwworm: herd inspections detected it 30 percent of the time at low fly density and every time at high density [B-1.4]. Mismatch: those are herd-level detection per round for a different fly, driven by how many animals were infested, not the per-animal chance the model uses.

What the sources do not tell us

How often a trained US inspector misses an infested animal in a chute: no study in the files measures it.

  • primary the source's own observations or measurements (an agency's own rule counts as primary for what the rule says)
  • secondary a review, textbook, compilation or agency summary citing others
  • news or anecdote a news story or an informal report
  • unclear none of these fits cleanly

A-1.7 García Coronado PL, Rosales-Martínez F, Zarate Triviño DG, et al. Natural occurrence of Cochliomyia...

Citation: García Coronado PL, Rosales-Martínez F, Zarate Triviño DG, et al. Natural occurrence of Cochliomyia hominivorax myiasis in surgically treated cattle under different macrocyclic lactone regimens. Front Anim Sci 2026;7:1839332.

Kind of evidence: experimental study also outbreak observation

Primary or not: primary The source's own trial measurements.

A 2025 to 2026 cattle trial in Chiapas, Mexico, with deliberate wounds checked daily. The earliest infestations, days 3 to 5, were in the ivermectin group, where the drug failed; the abstract gives two untreated controls infested on day 8 in the first period and one control case in the second.

Deliberate wounds in a treatment trial, but infestation came from wild flies (natural exposure).

Open the source

What it reports: Day 3 (2 animals), day 4 (4), day 5 (3) in the ivermectin group; day 4 and day 8 in controls; larvae 24 to 362 per wound at detection.

Abstract

Introduction The re-emergence of the New World screwworm ( Cochliomyia hominivorax ) in the Americas represents a renewed challenge for livestock production, animal welfare, and regional surveillance systems. Myiasis caused by this obligate parasitic fly produces rapid tissue destruction, severe inflammation, and intense pain in affected animals, making its prevention a critical component of welfare-oriented livestock management. Despite the widespread use of macrocyclic lactones within livestock health programs, field-based epidemiological evidence describing the occurrence of screwworm infestation under natural exposure conditions remains limited. This study aimed to document the natural occurrence and characteristics of Cochliomyia hominivorax myiasis in surgically treated cattle exposed under endemic conditions while receiving different macrocyclic lactone regimens. Methods An observational field study was conducted in southern Mexico using Brahman × Simbrah crossbred cattle (12–16 months old). Animals were evaluated in two observation periods (November–December 2025 and January 2026) and allocated into three groups: untreated control, ivermectin (3.5%), and doramectin (1%). A standardized full-thickness surgical wound was created in each animal to allow natural oviposition by screwworm flies. Cattle were monitored for 21 days post-surgery for the occurrence of myiasis, larval burden severity, larval developmental stages, and wound progression. Recovered larvae were morphologically and morphometrically examined to confirm species identity and developmental stage. Results During the first observation period, myiasis occurred predominantly in ivermectin-treated cattle, with infestations detected as early as three days post-surgery and larval burdens frequently classified as severe. Two animals in the untreated control group developed myiasis on Day eight, whereas no infestations were observed in the doramectin-treated group. In the second observation period, infestation frequency decreased, with one case detected in both the control and ivermectin groups and none in the doramectin group. All recovered larvae corresponded to late second (L2) and third (L3) instars of Cochliomyia hominivorax and exhibited preserved morphology and high motility. Discussion These findings highlight the multifactorial nature of screwworm infestation under natural field conditions, including environmental variables and pharmacological context. The study provides epidemiologically relevant evidence that can contribute to risk assessment of myiasis occurrence, improvement of livestock surveillance systems, and evidence-based decision-making in integrated screwworm control policies aimed at protecting livestock health and welfare in regions facing the re-emergence of Cochliomyia hominivorax .

A-1.8 Muchiut S, Miró MV, Anziani O, Nava S, Lifschitz A. Failure of doramectin and ivermectin in preventing...

Citation: Muchiut S, Miró MV, Anziani O, Nava S, Lifschitz A. Failure of doramectin and ivermectin in preventing Cochliomyia hominivorax myiasis in a subtropical region. Vet Parasitol 2025;334:110384.

Kind of evidence: experimental study also outbreak observation

Primary or not: primary The source's own trial measurements.

An Argentine trial on castrated calves, wounds inspected on days 3, 6 and 13 only: 9 of 10 untreated wounds showed screwworm myiasis at the day-3 inspection.

Deliberate wounds in a treatment trial, but infestation came from wild flies (natural exposure).

Open the source

What it reports: Controls 9/10 by day 3.

Abstract

The aim of this work is to present a case study where the failure of IVM 3.15 % and DRM 1 % to prevent natural infestations of C. hominivorax larvae in Argentina is investigated based on field efficacy tests and a pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic analysis. Thirty male crossbred Braford calves were randomly assigned to three experimental groups (n = 10), the IVM 3.15 % group (subcutaneously at 630 µg/kg), the DRM 1 % group (subcutaneously at 200 µg/kg) and the control group (saline solution subcutaneously). All treatments were performed at the time of castration surgery through a scrotal incision, and the wounds were exposed to natural infestations of C. hominivorax. Wound inspections were carried out on days 3, 6, and 13 post-treatments. Jugular blood samples were taken from experimental animals at 3- and 6-days post-treatment. In presence of C. hominivorax larvae, samples of both the larvae and wound secretions were collected in plastic vials on days 3 and 6 to measure concentrations of both drugs by high-performance liquid chromatography. On day 3 post-treatment, active myiasis was observed in 9 animals from the control group, 5 from the IVM 3.15 % group, and 6 from the DRM 1 % group. On day 6 post-treatment, 5 and 3 new myiasis were detected in the IVM 3.15 % and DRM 1 % group, respectively. No larvae were observed in the wounds on day 13 post-treatment. Interestingly, DRM concentrations tended to be higher in larvae compared to IVM on day 3 post-treatment (p = 0.051), and IVM plasma concentrations tended to be higher than those measured for DRM on day 6 (p = 0.087). There was a very strong correlation between DRM and IVM concentrations in plasma and wound secretions and larvae. The uptake of DRM from wound secretions to larvae was 83 % greater than that of IVM (p = 0.03). The results of this trial suggest the presence of C. hominivorax resistance to DRM and highlight concern about the lack of effectiveness of IVM 3.15 % in preventing C. hominivorax infestations.

Kind of evidence: model or expert estimate

Primary or not: unclear A modelling assumption cited to an earlier booklet, not an observation.

A 2026 compartmental model of the Mexico outbreak that assumes an infection lasting 15 to 17 days (2.1 weeks), cited to an earlier source not retrieved.

Open the source

What it reports: 15 to 17 d, taken as 2.1 weeks; cited to their reference 12 (Vargas-Terán 2020, not retrievable here; see paywalled table).

Abstract

An outbreak of New World screwworm has recently been spreading across Mexico, after more than 30 years of absence. The sterile insect technique, which consists of the massive release of sterilized males, has proven to be one of the most efficient methods for controlling the screwworm pest. However, given the limited number of sterile males available, improving the release strategy is critical. We propose a mathematical model of population dynamics adapted to the biology of Cochliomyia hominivorax and derive a feedback control function to determine the number of sterile males to release. We further construct a Luenberger observer to estimate wild fly populations from infected animal counts-the variable monitored by Mexican sanitary authorities-enabling field implementation of the control function. We show that eradication is achievable within approximately 60-100 weeks and that eradication time is governed primarily by the intrinsic biology of the system rather than by infestation magnitude. We then extend the model to a spatially explicit framework and show that when sterile male releases are applied at the outbreak focus and within a 120 km radius, eradication of the pest is attainable.

A-3.13 Moya-Borja GE, Oliveira CM, Muniz RA, Goncalves LC. Prophylactic and persistent efficacy of doramectin...

Citation: Moya-Borja GE, Oliveira CM, Muniz RA, Goncalves LC. Prophylactic and persistent efficacy of doramectin against Cochliomyia hominivorax in cattle. Vet Parasitol 1993;49(1):95-105.

Kind of evidence: experimental study

Primary or not: primary The source's own trial measurements.

A 1993 Brazilian trial (full text read): calves were given doramectin and, 2 hours later, two incisions each seeded with 50 first-stage larvae. Larvae were gone from treated wounds 24 to 48 hours after treatment and wounds healed by 96 to 120 hours. The dosing was preventive: the drug was in the animal before the larvae, so it does not time the clearing of an established wound.

Open the source

What it reports: First-instar larvae eliminated 24 to 48 h post-treatment; healing began at 24 h and was complete at 96 to 120 h; 100 percent of control incisions infested.

Abstract

Two prophylactic studies and one persistent efficacy study were conducted in Brazil to evaluate one injection of doramectin at a dose rate of 200 micrograms kg-1 against induced infestations of the New World screwworm, Cochliomyia hominivorax. In each prophylactic study, 12 calves were allocated to two groups of six animals. Six calves were treated with doramectin and six with saline. Two hours after treatment, animals were anesthetized and received two incisions, one in the shoulder and one in the rump. Each incision was then infested with 50 first instar larvae. In the persistent efficacy study, 24 calves were allocated to six groups (T1-T6) of four animals each. On the day of treatment, three groups (T1, T3 and T5) were treated with saline and three groups (T2, T4 and T6) with doramectin. All animals were anesthetized and received four incisions, one in the shoulder and one in the rump of each side. Each incision was then infested with 30 first instar larvae of C. hominivorax with the following schedule: T1 and T2 at Day 3, T3 and T4 at Day 7, and T5 and T6 at Day 14 post-treatment. Calves were observed daily and incisions evaluated for 8 days post-infection. Larvae that completed development and exited the wounds were collected and incubated to evaluate viability. In all experiments, doramectin was 100% efficacious in preventing screwworm infestation caused by field isolates of C. hominivorax. First instar larvae were eliminated from the incisions of doramectin-treated calves between 24 and 48 h post-treatment, and no third instar were recovered at any time. As a consequence, healing started at 24 h and was completed at 96-120 h post-infection. Screwworm infestations and viable third-instar larvae developed in all the incisions in non-treated calves, and healing did not begin until larvae had completed their normal life cycle and exited the wounds. The persistent efficacy of a single injection of doramectin extended beyond 14 days.

A-3.7 Rodriguez-Vivas RI, Cutolo AA, de Barros ATM, et al. Management practices for the control of Haematobia...

Citation: Rodriguez-Vivas RI, Cutolo AA, de Barros ATM, et al. Management practices for the control of Haematobia irritans, Dermatobia hominis, and Cochliomyia hominivorax in cattle across Latin America. Pathogens 2026;15(2):177.

Kind of evidence: review or textbook

Primary or not: secondary Review, textbook or factsheet summarizing others' work.

A 2026 review of fly control in Latin American cattle stating untreated infestations are usually fatal within 7 to 10 days.

Open the source

What it reports: Death 7 to 10 d after infestation if untreated.

Abstract

Bovines are suitable hosts and can be affected by fly infestations. Flies pose a significant threat to cattle livestock in Latin America (LA), causing substantial economic repercussions to animal production (reduced productivity, veterinary expenses, and decreased animal welfare) and damage to human health. The most important flies affecting cattle in Argentina, Brazil, Colombia, Mexico, and Uruguay are Haematobia irritans, Dermatobia hominis, and Cochliomyia hominivorax. Due to production losses and the consequent economic costs associated with these flies, control measures must be implemented, primarily relying on insecticidal products. However, decision-making for preventing and treating animals with insecticides varies due to differences in environmental conditions across countries and regions, production systems, animal populations, infestation levels, animal welfare, and the prevalence of myiasis, among other factors. Although insecticides remain the most effective option for fly control in cattle, resistant populations have developed, rendering them less effective. To overcome fly resistance to insecticides, non-chemical (mechanical, environmental, biological, and genetic) methods are being integrated into alternative control and eradication strategies. The use of integrated livestock fly control contributes to safeguarding animal, public, and environmental health. This review is designed to support individuals and institutions, both civil and governmental, addressing the ongoing challenge posed by flies affecting livestock.

A-5.1 Gutierrez AP, Ponti L, Arias PA. Deconstructing the eradication of New World screwworm in North America:...

Citation: Gutierrez AP, Ponti L, Arias PA. Deconstructing the eradication of New World screwworm in North America: retrospective analysis and climate warming effects. Med Vet Entomol 2019;33(2):282-295.

Kind of evidence: model or expert estimate

Primary or not: unclear Model output (the 14 day potential doubling) mixed with a field range cited from another study.

A 2019 population model of screwworm eradication giving a potential doubling time of 14 days and field doubling of 54 to 139 days in tropical populations.

The 54 to 139 d field figure is cited from Matlock and Skoda 2009 (C-1.2).

Open the source

What it reports: Potential doubling 14 d (temperate, favourable); field doubling 54 to 139 d (tropical endemic populations); R about 67 eggs per female per day at maximum; mated wild female half-life 3.7 d, mean age at wounds 7.5 d, maximum 21 d.

Abstract

Before its eradication from North America, the subtropical-tropical new world screwworm fly Cochliomyia hominivorax (Coquerel) invaded southwestern temperate areas of the U.S.A., where it caused myiasis in wildlife and livestock. Outbreaks of the fly occurred during years when adult migrants were carried northward on North American monsoon winds from the northern areas of Mexico and south Texas. We deconstruct, retrospectively, the biology and the effect of weather on the eradication of the fly in North America. Screwworm was found to be an ideal candidate for eradication using the sterile insect technique (SIT) because females mate only once, whereas males are polygynous, and, although it has a high reproductive potential, field population growth rates are low in tropical areas. In northern areas, eradication was enhanced by cool-cold weather, whereas eradication in tropical Mexico and Central America is explained by the SIT. Despite low average efficacy of SIT releases (approximately 1.7%), the added pressure of massive SIT releases reduced intrinsically low fly populations, leading to mate-limited extinction. Non-autochthonous cases of myiasis occur in North America and, if the fly reestablishes, climate warming by 2045-2055 will expand the area of favourability and increase the frequency and severity of outbreaks.
